entities.summary:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a seminal 1798 poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, born in the Early Modern era and influencing global literature with its haunting tale of guilt and redemption. Created in approximately 1797, this work showcases Coleridge's mastery of language and symbolism, transcending regional boundaries to become an iconic representation of human experience.

This masterpiece has had a lasting impact on the literary canon, contributing significantly to the Romantic movement and shaping the way writers approach themes of nature, morality, and the human condition. The poem's eerie and introspective tone has captivated readers for centuries, solidifying its place as a cornerstone of English literature.

One of the most striking aspects of this poem is its exploration of the consequences of humanity's actions on the natural world, which continues to resonate with contemporary environmental concerns. Through Coleridge's vivid imagery and masterful use of metaphor, 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' has left an indelible mark on our collective consciousness.

In conclusion, this poem remains a powerful testament to the enduring power of literature to shape our understanding of the world and ourselves, with its themes of guilt, redemption, and the interconnectedness of humanity and nature continuing to inspire new generations of readers and writers.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a major poem by the English Romantic poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834), first published in the joint collection Lyrical Ballads (1798) — co-authored with William Wordsworth and generally taken as the founding document of English Romanticism. In its final form (revised 1817, with marginal gloss added), the poem consists of seven parts and 625 lines in ballad form, narrating the supernatural voyage of an Ancient Mariner who shoots an albatross (a bird of good omen), brings a curse upon his ship, watches his shipmates die, and is condemned to wander the world, compelled to retell his tale.

The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a poem of sin, guilt, and penance — the shooting of the albatross is the Mariner's transgression against the natural order; the curse that follows (dead calm, the spectral ship, Death and Life-in-Death playing dice for the crew, the dead men's eyes staring) is the supernatural punishment; and the Mariner's penance is both the physical suffering on the becalmed ship and the perpetual compulsion to retell his story. The poem contains one of the most famous lines in English literature ('Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink') and the moral conclusion that divine love extends to all natural creatures ('He prayeth best, who loveth best / All things both great and small'). The marginal gloss added in 1817 creates an ironic commentary on the narrative, complicating the poem's meaning.

The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is the foundational text of English Romanticism's engagement with the sublime and the supernatural — with the terrifying, transgressive power of nature and the supernatural, the psychology of guilt and obsession, and the power of storytelling itself.
